newsitem.title: SPAIN: CiU ready to back Spain's 1998 budget - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: CiU ready to back Spain's 1998 budget - spokesman.

text.p: Catalan's Convergencia i Unio said on Thursday it was ready to back its minority government allies on the 1998 budget, which is designed to ensure Spain's prompt entry into European economic and monetary union.
"I think there won't be any problem that could put budget approval at risk," CiU economic spokesman Francesc Homs told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
The ruling minority Popular Party government needs the CiU's legislative votes to pass the budget. The CiU backs the PP in an alliance but is not part of the government.

"This is the last budget before the final decision will be taken. CiU is really looking for the peseta to enter the third phase of the monetary union. So we'll take all necessary measures to guarantee convergence with Europe," he said.
Although Spain will not be judged specifically on the 1998 budget deficit, it has vowed to prepare an austere budget to establish a track record of fiscal discipline.

In addition to bringing the 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product, Spain must meet criteria on long-term interest rates, debt, currency stability and inflation to ensure it can join at the launch of the common currency.

The new budget law, which foresees reducing the budget deficit to 2.5 percent of GDP from 3.0 percent this year, forecasts a 3.5 percent increase in 1998 GDP product and a 2.0 percent rise in consumer inflation, Homs said.

But despite broad agreement with the government on the budget, a draft of which the government is expected to present at the end of the month, the Catalan coalition stressed the need to boost health expenditures and public investment.
The committee studying the health issue already recognised expenditures for health financing would rise by 200 billion pesetas in 1998, which will be covered by an expected increase in revenues.
In addition, the government also projects additional spending of 100-120 billion pesetas for which the government must find alternative ways of financing.

According to a fiscal discipline plan, Spain already approved and presented to the European commission, the 1998 revenues are expected to rise 5.9 percent while 1998 expenditures are set to climb 4.7 percent.
Homs did not rule out the possibility reported recently by the Spanish press of raising special taxes, such as the ones on alcohol and tobacco.
"This may take place but it will not necessarily take place," he said. "We are awaiting the government's final decision on this."
Homs added the CiU expected a solid increase in public investment as well.

"In the next half of 1997 the government will have significant revenues from its privatisation process and the same will be true in 1998," he said, adding that this money would be used in the reduction of debt and in public investment. For public investment, 1997 has been a transition year.
"The 1998 budget will reveal increased privatisation receipts which will be used both to pay back debt and for public investment."
